reasons: accuracy: "That rule of never changing the patch" is an absolute; the glossary says nobody re-plugs channels without reason, and the same paragraph then talks about moving cables. reasons: accuracy: "The oldest answer is a slanted speaker" is a historical claim that may not hold ("The most common answer" is safe), and "while the stage stays free of feedback" in the closing is an absolute; clarity: paragraph 5 (split, separate console, outputs, sends, faders, click) is dense for a beginner; language: "The microphone picks up the wedge" read literally means the speaker itself, not its sound; glossary: "acoustic feedback" is a shortened form of "Acoustic Feedback / Howlround / Ringing" (an acceptable close match); opening_closing: the stage-concert opening sits close to sibling scenes in this batch, and the closing uses a short colon list

reasons: accuracy: "Some common microphones are known only by their model number" says "only", but these microphones are also known by their full names ("often known simply by their model number"); scope: the crew-people terms and the mixing-position terms ("mixing in a hole", "under a balcony", "bad seat") and the praise phrases ("that plays", "white glove") appear only in the closing or not at all; flow: tired ears are joined to the trouble paragraph with a weak link ("Trouble can also come from the crew's own ears"); language: that link sentence is slightly figurative; opening_closing: the backstage-crew scene is close to sibling 3640's scene, and the closing is a list of seven items

reasons: accuracy: "Most DJs keep reliable songs ready" is an unsupported "most" ("Many DJs"); scope: the large group of set types, events and roles (wedding and club sets, MC, karaoke, video jockey, battle formats) gets only one sentence about the shape of a night, and controller/software equipment is barely touched; flow: the scratching paragraph is a side branch between transitions and preparation; clarity: "This is called beatmatching" comes right after the small push, so a beginner may think beatmatching is only the push (the glossary defines it as matching speed and lining up beats); language: "more exciting" is used three times as a vague measure; glossary: the same "This" ambiguity against the beatmatching definition; opening_closing: the closing is a list of seven items

reasons: scope: the fire and emergency group (about 15% of 132 terms: PASS method, Class C fire, fire watch, hot work permit, smoke, theatrical fog, evacuation) gets only one sentence in paragraph 6, and incident or near-miss reporting is not mentioned; flow: paragraph 5 moves from protective equipment to 'Your body also matters' (heat, thirst, sleep) without a link, so it reads as a second idea; opening_closing: the closing is a colon list of six items in one 34-word sentence, and the standard asks for plain words with no list

reasons: accuracy: 'So it picks up all the sound around it' is an absolute (directional microphones reject sound from some directions), and 'A sensor worn against the throat works in the same way' is misleading, because a throat microphone senses vibration through the skin, not moving air the way a clip-on microphone does; scope: the pickup-problem terms (piezo quack, pickup loading, phase reversal, pickup height) and the ceiling-array and modeling terms are not touched, though the proportion is otherwise right; flow: paragraph 6 packs ultrasonic, infrasonic, always-on, optical, laser, ionic and particle-velocity designs into one paragraph; clarity: paragraph 6 asks a beginner to hold too many types at once; language: 'light' means 'not heavy' in paragraph 1 and then 'light' meaning illumination in paragraph 6, which can confuse a second-language reader; glossary: the throat-microphone description conflicts with the glossary ('feels that shaking through your skin'); opening_closing: paragraph 1 is three sentences and does not end on the topic's question, and the closing is a 31-word list
comment: The chain from the air-sensing microphone to the pickup, to the clip-on microphone, to the newer methods works well, and the space follows the term list, where pickups dominate. Two small accuracy slips and a crowded paragraph 6 keep it from an A. Weighted 4.1, grade B.

reasons: accuracy: 'A related tool, the expander, only turns quiet sounds down a little' understates it, because an expander's ratio sets how far it turns them down and that can be a lot; scope: ratio and knee are covered only as 'how much it turns the sound down', and multiband or frequency-dependent compression appears only in the closing list; flow: paragraph 6 joins three ideas (circuit designs, transient shaping, over-compression artifacts) with a weak 'Because they all…' link; clarity: 'Then you raise the level of the whole sound again' does not say why (the compressor made everything quieter), so a beginner may be puzzled; language: 'each have their own typical speed and tone' uses 'tone', a vague sound word left unexplained; glossary: the expander line is a little narrower than the glossary ('more gradually, by a set ratio'); opening_closing: the closing is a 42-word list of seven items
comment: The opening scene (keeping your hand on the knob) leads cleanly to threshold, compressor, limiter, gate and sidechain, and every term is named only after the reader needs it. Paragraph 6 and the list-style closing are the main weak points. Weighted 4.1, grade B.

reasons: (see the re-grade) accuracy: 'It points to files in a folder beside it' is a little wrong, because the glossary says the session document sits inside its session folder, not next to it; scope: automation (about 7%) gets one clause, and navigation, zoom and tools (about 10%) and fades or crossfades are not mentioned; flow: paragraph 7 squeezes automation, freeze and bounce into one sentence; clarity: 'Last, it remembers…' has an unclear 'it' after a paragraph about tempo; language: one 42-word sentence that is not a plain list, a simile ('works like a full studio'), and 'DAW' in the title is never spelled out; opening_closing: the lesson never says what the flashcards cover, and the last paragraph adds new ideas (automation, freeze, bounce) instead of closing; house_rules: the check script warns about the simile, the title abbreviation and two sentences over 30 words
comment: Re-graded after the fixes (ending split, DAW spelled out, flashcards closing added). The middle of the chain (session, tracks, recording, nondestructive editing, tempo grid) is clear and links well. The ending is the weak point: three new ideas are packed into one long sentence, and the lesson never says what the flashcards cover. Weighted 3.9, grade C: fix the ending before it is used as a model.

reasons: accuracy: 'A transistor unit reacts fast and makes the start of each hit more noticeable' is stated as always true, but a fast transistor compressor often reduces the start of a hit; add 'can' or say 'reacts fast' only; scope: the clipping-chain terms (clip-to-limit, serial clipping) and the technical-artifact group (oversampling, overshoot, hysteresis, logarithmic versus linear domains, about 10%) are not touched; flow: the last sentence of paragraph 3 adds transient tools and upward compression as side items; clarity: 'A stereo mix can also be divided into the center and the sides in the same way' is too short for a beginner to understand mid/side
comment: This is a true next-step topic, so the opening that recaps the core topic is allowed, and it ends on a clear question. The chain goes from deciding, to filtering, timing, circuit, splitting and serial work, then to the limiter, and every named term matches the glossary. Weighted 4.4, grade B.

reasons: (see the re-grade) accuracy: 'It depends mainly on distances' undersells mic direction, room reflections and the number of open mics (the glossary names all of them), and 'turns on each performer's wireless microphone only while that performer speaks or sings' is theater line-by-line practice but reads as true for every show; scope: the theater-production group (stage directions, cast, rehearsals, cues, load-in/strike, about a quarter of the 108 terms) gets one sentence about a stage manager, and the marching/parade and ceremony groups get two short sentences; flow: paragraph 6 (outdoor events) is a two-sentence side stop that could be moved or removed, and paragraph 7 (safety) is attached with no link to the planning thread; clarity: 'their own separate mixes' uses 'mix' without explaining it for a beginner; language: 'picks up' and 'goes around' are phrasal verbs whose meaning is not literal; glossary: the glossary says wind bleed 'is not real sound', but the lesson lists wind among the 'sounds' microphones pick up; opening_closing: the closing is a list of parts ('from feedback and open microphones to the stage, the show itself, events outside a hall, and safety').
comment: Re-graded after the fixes (gain before feedback, wind noise, theater-only mic practice, outdoor and safety paragraphs joined). The feedback, open-microphone and spill chain is clear and accurate, and it opens from a good everyday scene. The second half is weaker: the large theater-production group is squeezed into a few sentences, and the outdoor and safety paragraphs sit beside the chain instead of growing from it.

reasons: scope: most of the 108 terms are console and software product families, and the lesson covers them only as 'main types of digital consoles' in the closing (correct, since brand names are not allowed, but the console-family group has no paragraph of its own); flow: paragraph 5 puts three separate ideas together (fader layers, helper tools, tablet control); clarity: 'preamplifier', 'faders' and 'input level' are used without plain explanation for a beginner; opening_closing: the lesson opens by pointing to the analog topic, which is only allowed for a true next-step topic, and analog and digital live sound are arguably sibling topics a learner can take in any order; the closing is a list of seven items.
comment: This is an accurate, well-built picture of how a split digital system works, from the surface through the stage box, latency, layers and scenes, and every named term matches its glossary meaning. The weak points are a packed fifth paragraph, a few undefined console words, and a list-style closing.

This is the strongest lesson in the batch. It follows one clear thread (place the speakers, lift them safely, aim them, test the plan, fill the gaps), the rigging safety rules come early and are correct, and every named term agrees with the glossary.

reasons: accuracy: 'It matters most where subwoofers ... overlap with the main speakers' is an absolute, and main-to-delay and main-to-fill alignment matter just as much ('It is especially important where...' would be true); flow: the paragraphs open with a 'First... Next... Next...' sequence, which sits close to the banned enumerating pattern; clarity: 'a measurement with the same level at every frequency often gives listeners too many high frequencies' is hard for a beginner to follow without knowing what a flat response is; language: 'tune toward a planned shape' uses 'shape' figuratively for a frequency curve; opening_closing: the closing is a seven-item list.
comment: This is an accurate, well-ordered tour of verification, measuring, timing, tone and listening checks, and its prerequisite opening fits a true next-step topic. The small fixes are one absolute about subwoofer alignment, the 'First/Next' scaffolding, and a list-style closing.

reasons: accuracy: 'uses a steady radio wave to carry the sound' conflicts with the later 'changing radio wave', and 'as a changing radio wave or as digital data' suggests digital systems do not use a radio wave (both do; the difference is how the wave is changed); flow: paragraph 5 jumps from reception to transmitter settings with no link, and battery safety is added at the very end of paragraph 6; clarity: paragraph 4 packs six ideas into one paragraph (distance loss, body absorption, reflections, directional antennas, shared antenna box, diversity); language: 'steady' and 'changing' radio wave can confuse a literal reader; opening_closing: the opening (a singer on stage) is the same kind of scene as sibling 3560 (a student singing at a concert).
comment: This lesson covers a very large topic broadly and correctly, from radio laws through coordination, antennas, settings and show checks, and its named terms match the glossary. It is the densest lesson in the batch, and the 'steady versus changing radio wave' wording should be made consistent.

reasons: accuracy: "A cable takes the whole signal out of a channel, through the processor, and back in" makes an insert sound like one cable, when it is a send and a return; "The preamps and converters are usually built into one box" is true of home and project studios, but many professional rooms use separate units; scope: the monitor calibration and controller group (about 15% of terms) gets two thin sentences with the controller unnamed, and stems, print, bounce and double tracking appear only as "the main ways of recording"; flow: the outboard paragraph sits between the preamp and the headroom and converter paragraph, so "Every stage has a maximum level" does not grow out of the processor paragraph; clarity: eight paragraphs at 478 words, with seven terms or near-terms (preamp, mic preamp, audio interface, buffer size, direct monitoring, cue mix, overdub); language: "So many interfaces send..." can be read as "a great number of interfaces" rather than "therefore, many interfaces", and "A control box" is vague; opening_closing: the closing's "the main ways of recording" adds an idea the body never set up
comment: A clear, accurate route from the microphone to the file, with good beginner explanations of buffer size, direct monitoring and the cue mix. It is near the word limit, and the monitoring and outboard parts are a little thin and out of order. Weighted 4.1, grade B.

reasons: flow: paragraph 5 ("The work also passes between several people.") packs client approval, version names, mix handoff and remote sessions into one run of short facts with no link between them; clarity: six named terms (take, pickup request, comp take, take sheet, recall sheet, red-light fever), the most the standard allows, four of them in two paragraphs; language: "The players matter too" and "The work also passes between several people" are vague when read literally; opening_closing: the closing is a long list of seven items ("from planning the day and helping performers to takes, joining the best parts, notes, approvals, remote sessions and backups")
comment: A strong, accurate before-during-after chain that covers every large group in this broad topic, including backups and remote work. The only weak spot is the crowded handoff and remote paragraph. Weighted 4.5, grade A.

reasons: accuracy: "often from a truck or a portable rack" overstates trucks (many concerts are recorded from a stage rack or the mixing position), and "Verses tell the story" is stated as always true; scope: live and remote recording is about a quarter of the terms but gets half a paragraph; flow: paragraph 6 joins two unrelated ideas (studio takes and overdubs, then concert recording), and "A concert is also recorded..." jumps without a link; clarity: "kit" and "drum fills" are used without explanation; language: "A loud kit", "the click" (short form) and "more intense" (vague) are unclear for a second-language reader; opening_closing: the closing is a 32-word list sentence that the script flags
comment: Accurate on arrangement, bed tracks and spill, and the glossary agrees throughout. But the live-recording part is squeezed into the end of a paragraph about takes, which breaks the chain. Weighted 4.0, grade B.
fixes: flow (3): Quote: "The band plays the song several times, and the engineer marks the best attempt. Later, other parts are added over the bed tracks, one at a time. A concert is also recorded with the band playing together, often from a truck or a portable rack, but nothing can be repeated." Problem: the paragraph changes topic halfway, from studio takes and overdubs to concert recording, with no link between them, so the live-recording group arrives as an afterthought. Fix: move the first two sentences to the end of paragraph 4 (after "...so later parts match in time."), and open paragraph 6 with: "A concert is also recorded with the band playing together, but nothing can be repeated. The recording equipment is often placed in a portable rack or a truck near the stage." Keep the splitter and redundant-recording sentences after it.

reasons: accuracy: "Electric organs mix tones with sliders" is true of tonewheel organs but not of all electric organs (needs "Many electric organs"), and "Until it is done, the rattle stays in every recording" is an absolute; flow: the body is a tour of instrument families, and paragraphs 3 to 5 could be reordered without loss; paragraph 4's frame ("change with the way the player plays") does not fit its harmonica and accordion sentence; clarity: paragraph 4 packs violin, brass, mutes, harmonica and accordion into one paragraph; language: "settings for pitch and touch" (touch means velocity response) is unclear when read literally; opening_closing: the closing is a list, and banjos and harps appear there for the first time
comment: An accurate, well-grounded lesson that ties each family to how it makes and sends out its sound, and that closes the opening's setup idea. It reads more as a tour than a chain, and one paragraph is crowded. Weighted 4.3, grade B.

reasons: flow: drum bleed is added at the end of the cymbal paragraph in two short sentences, so the step from choosing cymbals to bleed feels abrupt; clarity: "a soft felt one" uses felt without explaining it, and "gel pad" is not explained; language: "rings" and "the drum's own note" are mildly figurative for a literal reader; opening_closing: "Imagine a drummer in a recording room" is the same kind of scene as sibling 3840 ("Imagine a singer in a small recording room"), which the owner's rule forbids, and the closing is a list

reasons: scope: filter design families (Butterworth, Bessel, Chebyshev, elliptic, FIR/IIR, biquad, all-pass) are about a quarter of the 333 terms but get two short sentences, and measurement/room correction appears only in the closing; flow: 'Filter designs also differ.' is added to the end of the timing paragraph without growing from it; clarity: paragraph 4 packs phase shift, linear phase, latency, pre-ringing and filter trade-offs into a few sentences; language: 'balances an even level, a steep slope and even timing' and 'give a sound a new character' are abstract or vague for a literal reader; opening_closing: the closing is a list of six items

reasons: flow: paragraph 7 (unnatural reverbs) is a short add-on that could be moved without breaking the chain; clarity: 'sends the sound through short delays whose output is sent back into their input' is hard for a beginner on first read
comment: A clear, accurate lesson that covers the whole topic: the older machines, the computer methods, the controls, modulation, use in a mix and creative uses. The language is plain and literal, and the terms agree with the glossary.

reasons: clarity: paragraph 5 puts the Haas widening, chorus and flanging into one dense paragraph; language: the opening question is long (26 words), 'help the music' is vague, and the check script flagged 'listening' (its literal use here is fine); opening_closing: the opening scene (a sound made in a space comes back as an echo) is the same kind of scene as the sibling Reverb lesson (a clap in an empty hall), and the closing is a list of six items
comment: A strong chain from the basic repeat to feedback, storage, timing, very short moving delays and ducking. It is accurate and covers the whole topic. The opening repeats the sibling Reverb lesson's kind of scene, which the owner's rules forbid.
fixes: Quote: "Imagine you shout once toward a large stone wall far away. A moment later, you hear your voice again, a little quieter." -> Problem: the Reverb lesson (3370) in the same field also opens with a sound made in a space that comes back ('Imagine clapping once in an empty concert hall'), and the owner's 8c rule says sibling lessons never open with the same kind of scene. -> Fix: "Imagine a guitarist plays one note, and the same note sounds again a moment later, a little quieter, then again, in time with the drums." Then change the next sentence to "Many songs use repeats of this kind on purpose, made by equipment." reasons: accuracy: 'In earlier topics, effects mostly corrected problems' assumes a study order that learners may not follow, and it is not true of reverb or delay; scope: phaser and the spectral effects (spectral freeze, cross-synthesis, shifting, about 9% of the terms) are not mentioned; flow: paragraph 2 adds the telephone effect and ring modulation as side items after saturation; clarity: 'multiply two sounds' and 'new frequencies appear above each note' are abstract for a beginner; language: 'loses its natural character' is vague; opening_closing: the opening points to earlier topics and repeats the Welcome text's idea of 'magic, not correction'
comment: A well-linked lesson from distortion to modulation, pitch and voice tools, edits and transitions, and the named terms agree with the glossary. The opening depends on earlier topics and repeats the Welcome text's idea, and the spectral effects are missing.
fixes: Quote: "In earlier topics, effects mostly corrected problems, but here they are part of the music." -> Problem: learners can study topics in any order (owner 8c), reverb and delay are not only corrections, and the sentence repeats the Welcome text's idea ('a mix needs magic, not correction'), which goes against rule 22. -> Fix: "Here the effects are not hidden. They are a part of the music that you can hear." Quote: "But a voice raised in pitch often loses its natural character." -> Problem: 'natural character' is vague for a literal reader. -> Fix: "But a voice raised in pitch often stops sounding like the same person."

reasons: accuracy: 'Grouping also shows where sounds share frequencies' is a stretch, because a bus does not show anything, and 'it also reduces the sharp start of each drum hit' is an absolute (it depends on the attack setting); flow: that same sentence is a forced bridge from bus processing to ducking; clarity: the bus paragraph also carries the kick and bass masking and frequency-selective ducking; language: 'Grouping also shows' reads as personification; opening_closing: the closing is a two-sentence list of six items
comment: It covers the whole topic in proportion: parallel blends and their timing risk, layering, buses, kick and bass ducking, and processing order. Starting points are given as common practice. One weak bridge sentence and a small absolute are the main issues.

reasons: flow: the licensing paragraph ('A plugin also needs permission to run') does not grow from the opening question about running inside another program at the correct time; clarity: paragraph 6 reads as several lists of variants (consoles, compressors, tape machines; amplifiers, cabinets, pedals, microphones; repair tasks), which the standard leaves to the flashcards; opening_closing: the closing is a list of five items
comment: An accurate, brand-free picture of a topic that is mostly product names. It explains formats, hosts, latency and compensation, processing power, licenses and the functional groups that the product names belong to, and every named term matches the glossary.

reasons: accuracy: 'it has thick wire and no shield' is an absolute; speaker cable usually has no shield, and the reason given (high power) is only part of the story; scope: the snake/multicore/fan-out group (about 10% of terms) gets only one sentence; flow: paragraph 4 is about cable length, then jumps to digital reflections ('Fast digital signals need a cable that matches the equipment electrically'), which is not about length; safety handling comes last even though the opening question names it; clarity: impedance matching and reflected pulses are a step beyond a beginner; language: phrasal verbs 'pick up noise' and 'cared for', and the personification in 'Every cable must also last, and never hurt anyone'; opening_closing: the closing is an eight-item list of flashcard contents
comment: A clear and accurate tour of what is inside a cable, noise, cable types, data cable and safe handling, with every named term matching the glossary. Small absolutes, one jump inside the length paragraph and a list-style closing keep it from an A.

reasons: scope: direct boxes (DI, active and passive direct box) are not mentioned; punch-down blocks and the furniture group get only a clause or the closing; flow: paragraph 5 moves from the studio control room in the opening to a stage without a link; clarity: the half-normal sentence ('a plug in the upper socket only receives a copy of the signal and leaves the default path working') is dense for a beginner; language: 8 sentences over 20 words (at the limit), plus 'get into'; opening_closing: the closing names 'the blocks where building cables end', which the body never introduced
comment: Covers racks, cooling and power, patch bay normalling, splitting and building pathways accurately, and the terms agree with the glossary. The stage-splitting paragraph breaks the studio thread, and the patch bay detail is heavy for a first read.

reasons: flow: paragraph 5 ('A touring show sends its paperwork before it arrives') starts a new scene with no link to the repair thread of paragraphs 1-4; clarity: paragraphs 5 and 6 end in long lists (frequencies, cases, songs; date, place, time stamp, format, microphones, processors); language: the closing clause 'let others build, repair and name the people who made the work later' is awkward to read literally
comment: Covers the whole topic: signal drawings, physical drawings, labels and schedules, show paperwork and metadata, with all six named terms matching the glossary. The only real weakness is the unlinked jump to touring paperwork.

reasons: flow: paragraph 3 bundles many separate ideas (input, level, headphones, punch-in, pre-record buffer, slate mic, timecode), and the history paragraph steps backward before the file paragraph moves forward again; clarity: paragraph 3 names two terms and explains timecode in quick succession
comment: A strong lesson with a clear phone-recording opening, a whole-topic chain (machine, controls, storage, older media, files and codecs) and accurate codec and lossy wording. Paragraph 3 is crowded.

reasons: flow: paragraph 6 joins two unrelated ideas (other systems and shared standards, then protection and domains); clarity: paragraph 4 packs flows, flow limits, capacity, the receive wait and quality of service into one paragraph; opening_closing: the closing paragraph opens with a new idea (the troubleshooting order: link light, cable, names, subscriptions) before saying what the flashcards cover

reasons: scope: the monitoring and network-management group (about 11%, the title's third part) gets two short sentences; jitter and world time standards appear only in the closing; clarity: 'needs a matching end plug, so the signal does not reflect back' assumes the reader knows about signal reflection; language: mild personification in 'A small clock inside it decides' and in devices that 'compare' and 'choose'; opening_closing: the closing adds topics the body never introduced ('small timing errors, world time standards')
comment: An excellent single line of thought from clock slip to a leader clock, word clock, the network grandmaster, redundancy and monitoring, with accurate claims and terms that match the glossary. Network management is thin for a part of the title.

reasons: scope: the addressing and protocol-layer group (IP, DHCP, ARP, TCP/UDP, OSI layers) gets one sentence, and Power over Ethernet is absent; clarity: 'a speed and a sending mode' leaves 'mode' unexplained, so the duplex-mismatch point is hard for a beginner to follow; language: informal 'can look fine' and mild personification in 'live sound cannot wait'
comment: A well-built next-step lesson that runs from packets and cables through switches, loops, multicast and managed switches to the latency budget, with accurate, hedged claims. Addressing and protocols are under-covered for their size.

reasons: accuracy: 'A very thin oxide layer stores the most charge for its size' is an absolute, and supercapacitors (EDLC, ultracapacitor) in this topic's own list store more; scope: units (farad, henry, picofarad, microfarad) and the standard-value system are never touched, and the materials and sensor group gets only one crowded sentence; flow: paragraph 6 jumps from diodes to heat and light sensors to magnetic shielding metals to crystals, with no link between them; clarity: 'the oxide type' is said to have a liquid that dries out, but the lesson never says this type contains a liquid, and paragraph 6 packs too many ideas together; language: 'carry sudden short jumps in voltage away from chips' is hard to read literally; opening_closing: the closing is a six-item list of what the flashcards cover
comment: A clear, accurate walk from resistor to capacitor to inductor that a beginner can follow. The last body paragraph turns into a list of unrelated parts and materials, and one 'most' claim is not true for this topic.
fixes: FLOW (paragraph 6): "Other parts change their resistance with heat or light. Materials also matter. Some metals block magnetic hum, some crystals turn pressure into voltage, and a quartz crystal vibrates at one exact rate, so it keeps accurate time." -> problem: three unrelated ideas follow the diodes with no link, so the paragraph could be split anywhere -> fix: "Some passive parts react to the world around them. Some change their resistance with heat or light. Some crystals turn pressure into a voltage. A quartz crystal vibrates at one exact rate, so it keeps accurate time. Even the metal around a part matters, because some metals block magnetic hum."  Related accuracy fix (score 4): "A very thin oxide layer stores the most charge for its size." -> "A very thin oxide layer stores a large charge for its size."
